title: Premium E-commerce Storefront
summary: A premium skincare storefront built around strong product presentation, mobile-first layouts and a streamlined path to purchase.
overview: How a premium skincare brand translates in-store trust into a WordPress storefront: generous product photography space, clear benefit hierarchy, and a checkout path that never loses the customer's momentum.
problem: Beauty and skincare shoppers decide with their eyes first and their questions second. Storefronts that hide benefits behind generic templates lose people on the product page — before price even becomes a factor.
audience: Independent skincare and cosmetics brands selling directly to consumers, primarily on mobile devices.
role: Lead — information architecture, interface design, WordPress implementation approach and performance plan.
designDecisions: Benefit-led product pages: outcome first, ingredients second, social proof third.
A restrained palette so product photography carries the visual weight.
Sticky add-to-cart bar on mobile, where most of the traffic lands.
Collection templates designed for scanning — price, size and key claim always visible.
implementation: Modular Elementor sections with a locked type scale so editors cannot break the hierarchy.
Lazy-loaded media below the fold and compressed hero imagery to protect LCP.
Semantic templates for homepage, collection, product and cart to keep crawl paths clean.
Accessible form controls, focus states and contrast across the purchase flow.

sections.label: Homepage
body: Hero with a single, confident promise and one primary action.
Ingredient and benefit storytelling broken into short, scannable blocks.
Best-seller grid that adapts from four columns to a swipeable two-up on mobile.

sections.label: Product page
body: Large imagery, benefit bullets above the fold, and an always-reachable purchase panel.
FAQ and shipping expectations resolved before the customer has to ask.

sections.label: Product listing
body: Filterable collection layout with clear price, size and skin-concern signals.
Consistent card rhythm so the grid stays calm even with heavy imagery.

sections.label: Mobile layout
body: Single-column flow, thumb-reachable actions and no horizontal scrolling at any breakpoint.

sections.label: Design rationale
body: Every layout choice answers one question: does this help the shopper decide faster?
The system stays deliberately quiet so photography and copy do the selling.

lessons: Product pages convert on clarity, not on decoration — the design system had to enforce that.
Editor-friendly modals matter as much as customer-facing ones; a beautiful site that editors break in week two fails.

title: Shopify Commerce Experience
summary: An online store with polished collection pages, compelling product presentation and a simplified purchasing journey.
overview: A storefront that explores how Shopify's native strengths — fast checkout, clean collections, reliable merchandising — can be shaped into a distinctive brand experience without fighting the platform.
problem: Many Shopify stores look identical because they start from the same theme. The challenge is expressing brand character while keeping the platform's conversion advantages intact.
audience: Small and growing product brands that need a storefront that looks custom but stays maintainable.
role: Lead — storefront structure, theme customisation approach and merchandising patterns.
designDecisions: Collection pages designed as editorial spreads rather than plain product grids.
Product cards carry one clear claim and one clear price — nothing else competes.
A quiet, high-contrast type system so seasonal campaigns can recolour the store safely.
implementation: Section-based layout so merchants can rearrange the homepage without a developer.
Responsive image handling and deferred non-critical scripts to protect load speed.
Consistent product card component reused across collection, search and related blocks.
Accessible navigation and form controls throughout the buying journey.

sections.label: Homepage
body: Brand statement, featured collection and a single clear path into shopping.

sections.label: Collection page
body: Balanced grid density, sticky filters on mobile and always-visible pricing.

sections.label: Product details
body: Imagery-first layout with sizing, shipping and returns answers close to the buy button.

sections.label: Responsive layouts
body: Design reviewed at 360px, 768px and 1440px before any feature is considered finished.

lessons: Working with a platform's grain beats working against it — most customisation value came from layout and content systems, not from rewriting core behaviour.

title: Conversion Tracking Architecture
summary: A walkthrough of how browser events, server events and deduplication work together into one trustworthy measurement layer.
overview: A reference build documenting an end-to-end measurement architecture: what fires in the browser, what fires on the server, how the two are matched, and how an analyst confirms everything is healthy.
problem: Browser-only tracking degrades as privacy controls tighten. When Pixel events and server events are wired separately — or wired twice — reporting becomes either incomplete or double-counted.
audience: Marketing teams and business owners running paid social who need measurement they can defend in a reporting meeting.
role: Tracking architect — event taxonomy, browser and server wiring plan, validation workflow.
designDecisions: One event taxonomy used by browser, server and dashboards — names and parameters never drift.
Event IDs generated once and shared by both channels so deduplication is deterministic.
A validation checklist treated as part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.
implementation: Browser Pixel fires page view and engagement events with stable event IDs.
Server-side Conversions API sends the same events with matching IDs and hashed customer parameters.
Deduplication confirmed in Events Manager by checking event count parity.
GA4 receives a parallel, privacy-conscious event stream for analytics reporting.

sections.label: Tracking architecture
body: Diagram of sources: site events → browser Pixel and server CAPI → Meta event deduplication → reporting.

sections.label: Event flow
body: Purchase, lead, add-to-cart and key micro-conversions mapped end to end.

sections.label: Deduplication diagram
body: event_id and event_source_url shown as the matching keys between browser and server.

sections.label: Event validation checklist
body: Each event verified for presence, parameters, deduplication and alert configuration.

sections.label: Example dashboard
body: Illustrative dashboard layout showing how event health is reported after launch.

lessons: Most tracking problems are naming and identity problems — fixing the taxonomy resolves a surprising share of broken reports.
Measurement should be documented for the person who inherits it, not just configured for the person who built it.

title: Full-Stack Business Dashboard
summary: An application dashboard for managing business information, products and operational data — including the states most demos skip.
overview: An operations dashboard focused on the unglamorous parts that decide whether a tool gets used: readable tables, fast filters, honest loading states and errors that explain themselves.
problem: Internal tools are usually demoed on happy paths with perfect data. Real usage means empty tables, slow responses, partial failures and people in a hurry.
audience: Small business teams managing catalogues, orders or operational records day to day.
role: Full-stack engineer — data model, API integration, interface system and state handling.
services: Loading, error and empty state design
designDecisions: Tables are the product: dense, keyboard-navigable, with predictable column alignment.
Filters live in the URL so a view can be shared or refreshed without losing state.
Every async surface ships four states — loading, empty, error and success — designed together.
implementation: Server Components for data-heavy views, Client Components only where interaction demands it.
Optimistic UI for lightweight edits with rollback on failure.
Accessible dialogs, toasts and focus management across keyboard and screen reader flows.
Responsive table strategy: horizontal scroll with frozen key columns on small screens.

sections.label: Dashboard
body: Summary metrics and recent activity without vanity charts.

sections.label: Data tables
body: Sortable, filterable and paginated records with clear bulk actions.

sections.label: Filters
body: Composable filters reflected in the URL for shareable views.

sections.label: API integration
body: Typed fetch layer with explicit error boundaries per resource.

sections.label: States
body: Loading skeletons, actionable error messages and empty states that teach the next step.

lessons: Designing the error state first changes the architecture — it surfaces which failures actually matter.

title: High-Impact Landing Page
summary: A conversion-focused landing page for a digital product or e-commerce offer — message match from ad to CTA.
overview: A landing page built for paid traffic: one audience, one promise, one primary action, and every section answering the next objection in order.
problem: Most landing pages fail because they mirror the homepage. Visitors arriving from an ad expect the promise they clicked — not a company overview.
audience: Campaign traffic from Meta Ads arriving cold on a single offer.
role: Designer and developer — message architecture, page build, and measurement wiring.
designDecisions: Headline reuses the ad's exact promise so message match is immediate.
Single primary CTA repeated at natural decision points — never competing buttons.
FAQ placed just before the final CTA to resolve the objections that stall conversions.
Fast first paint by design: no heavy hero media, no blocking scripts above the fold.
implementation: Static-first rendering with interactivity layered on top.
Form and CTA events pushed to Pixel and GA4 with consistent event names.
Mobile-first layout reviewed at 360px before desktop polish.
Accessible contrast, focus order and label associations across every control.

sections.label: Hero
body: Promise, proof element and the primary action visible without scrolling.

sections.label: Value proposition
body: What it is, who it is for, and what changes after buying.

sections.label: Benefits
body: Outcome-led blocks instead of feature dumps.

sections.label: Offer structure
body: Price, what is included, and risk reversal in one clear block.

sections.label: FAQs
body: Real objections answered plainly, structured with semantic markup.

sections.label: Primary CTA
body: A final action block with contact alternatives for higher-consideration buyers.

lessons: Cutting sections is the highest-leverage design decision on a landing page.
Tracking belongs in the launch checklist — retrofitting events after a campaign starts loses data.

title: Immersive Creative Portfolio
summary: The portfolio you are looking at — cinematic art direction, layered environmental storytelling and modern web animation, built to stay fast and accessible.
overview: This site itself: a Pandora-inspired digital ecosystem where every section is a different region of one world, built as a real Next.js application rather than a video.
problem: Developer portfolios tend to look interchangeable. The challenge was to create something memorable that still loads fast, reads clearly, and converts a visitor into an enquiry.
audience: Businesses evaluating web developers who want evidence of both engineering discipline and design taste.
role: Designer and engineer — art direction, component system, animation architecture, performance and accessibility.
designDecisions: Environments are drawn with layered SVG and gradients — original artwork, no borrowed film assets.
Motion budget set per element: ambient drift for the world, quick reveals for content.
Bright cyan reserved for interaction; large surfaces stay deep and calm for contrast and taste.
Reduced-motion and mobile paths simplify particles, parallax and blur instead of shipping them everywhere.
implementation: Server Components by default; Client Components only for menus, filters, theme and animation triggers.
Parallax driven by transform and opacity through Motion, gated by reduced-motion and viewport width.
Ambient particles are static markup animated in CSS — no canvas loop, no continuous JS.
Semantic structure, skip link, focus management and WCAG-conscious contrast throughout.

sections.label: Hero environment
body: Layered forest, floating mountains, mist and a controlled headline reveal.

sections.label: Scroll transitions
body: Each section shifts lighting and depth while staying one continuous world.

sections.label: Interactive components
body: Skill ecosystem, project filters and theme toggle — all keyboard-operable.

sections.label: Responsive behaviour
body: Parallax and particle counts reduced on small screens and low-powered devices.

lessons: Cinematic does not have to mean heavy — most of the atmosphere comes from layering and timing, not from expensive effects.
A strong theme system forces better token discipline than hard-coding colours ever does.
